task.background: Navigate a boat through mandatory waypoint circles IN ORDER, then stop inside the final circle. There is no prescribed path between points: choose your own efficient path. All positions and directions use FIXED geographic east/north axes, NEVER the bow or camera. No obstacles, wind or sideways drift are simulated. The world pauses while you decide. Each waypoint has a MAXIMUM permitted actual speed while passing its circle; this is only a ceiling, not a desired speed or a speed to match. Slower is allowed. You choose one nonnegative target ground speed and one ABSOLUTE course, clockwise from north. The simulator actuator turns the boat smoothly; a course command is not an instantaneous movement direction.

execution.frame: Fixed east/north; course 0=N,90=E,180=S,270=W. No bow-relative positions.
execution.forecast: Approximate ground-velocity forecast; assumes zero initial course rotation and a fresh response. Unknown startup direction uses candidate direction. Not a guarantee.

action.instructions: Choose ONE command. Treat a predicted passing_speed_above_ceiling=true as a violation to avoid. Speed ceilings are mandatory and take priority over faster progress. An EXCEEDS warning must not be traded for speed. If excess is already unavoidable from current motion, brake strongly to reduce it rather than accelerate. Never accelerate hard near a circle merely because this single action stops short of entering it. Use the longer same-command preview to anticipate the following action. On final approach use a slow controlled entry under its ceiling, then stop. Do not stop far outside and then restart at full speed: approach at a low nonzero speed instead. First pass the current mandatory circle without exceeding its speed ceiling. Future points are previews only; never skip the current point. Brake BEFORE entering a slower waypoint circle: the ceiling applies to ACTUAL speed, not commanded speed. Because forecasts are approximate, begin braking with spatial margin: do not rely on barely meeting the ceiling at the exact boundary. Use approach_margin_speed_above_ceiling as an early-braking warning, especially with residual high speed or a course change. The extra approach margin is a conservative cue only; the actual arrival radius and speed ceiling are unchanged. Account for speed and course transition durations. A zero-speed command brakes over time, not instantly. Intermediate waypoints require no stop. Once a waypoint is passed, proceed to the next one; keep respecting the previous ceiling until you leave its circle. If recently_passed_circle exists, its exit ceiling is still ACTIVE even though the target switched. A candidate with previous_circle_speed_above_ceiling=true accelerates too early: delay acceleration until outside. The final waypoint requires being inside AND slow enough; entering quickly is not completion. A stopped boat outside the final circle must approach instead of repeatedly stopping. Avoid needless stops, crawling, detours or alternating large course changes. After a turn settles, increase speed again when feasible; do not keep the slowest startup speed for a long clear approach. Among commands that respect active speed ceilings and reach the correct circle, compare distance_reduction_m: prefer useful larger progress over repeatedly crawling for a negligible endpoint improvement. Travel fast when far enough away, aligned, and able to brake before the next circle; slow for turns or nearby targets. For an off-axis target, diagonal motion or alternating adjacent compass headings can reach it. Inspect the predicted endpoint distance and entry facts, but these are APPROXIMATIONS from ground velocity: bow direction, yaw rate and actuator progress are unavailable. In particular startup and sharp turns may differ. If the waypoint is behind the current movement, slow before turning back. When very close or already inside the final circle, prefer braking to zero over another accelerating move. All candidates remain available: no local controller selects, ranks or filters your choice.
